A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Frankentexts research. Their main text, figures, tables, algorithm and complete appendices are readable and support matching retained, relocated, revised and added material.

before.justification: V1 reports original generation and detector evaluations, human assessments, and ablation results in Table 2, Section 4 and the appendices.

after.justification: V3 retains original empirical results and reports additional model comparisons, writing-quality measurements, human ratings, snippet-budget experiments and agentic retrieval results.

M1.justification: The core drafting, optional revision and polishing procedure remains unchanged. However, v3 Section 2 and Appendix L add an agentic generation branch in which the model searches and fetches additional snippets through MCP, with roughly 20 tool calls. This introduces interactive retrieval during generation, distinct from v1 Appendix I's one-shot retrieval of 1,500 prompt-similar paragraphs.

E1.justification: The narrative coverage remains: Mythos/Books3, Tell Me a Story, nonfiction news, single-book sourcing and longer outputs all appear in both versions. The limited additional data use is v3 Section 3.3's calibration of reward thresholds using 2,700 GPT-4 evaluations from MT-bench. NoveltyBench supplies metrics rather than a new narrative prompt dataset; larger snippet pools and MCP otherwise reuse existing coverage.

E2.justification: Within the main vanilla-versus-Frankentext comparisons, v3 replaces o4-mini and Claude 3.7 Sonnet with GPT-5 and Claude 4 Sonnet, and removes non-thinking Qwen3-32B (Tables 2 and 8). V3's shortened Qwen label denotes the retained thinking configuration. Older configurations still appear in retained appendix plots. Pangram, Binoculars and FastDetectGPT remain evaluated; moving detector results to Table 8 does not remove those comparators.

E3.justification: V3 adds Distinct3, Utility3, surprise and five-dimension LLM ratings, with three generations per prompt for diversity evaluation. The human pairwise study changes from 30 standard Gemini pairs assessed using the earlier coherence/relevance/authorship rubric to 20 pairs using 5,000 snippets and 1–7 quality ratings, with randomized presentation. Snippet-budget testing is also revised: v1 Appendix I describes approximately 100,000 paragraphs for maximal context, whereas v3 specifies 5,000 and 10,000 snippets. These are changes in reported settings, not evidence that an identical experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: V3 adds expanded snippet-budget analysis, MCP retrieval versus random sampling, and an alternative-judge analysis (Sections 4.2 and 4.4, Appendix Q). V1 Appendix I/Figure 14's standalone sentence-granularity and static relevant-paragraph ablations are absent; the MCP experiment uses a different retrieval procedure. Copy-rate sensitivity, editing removal, single-book sourcing, longer-output analysis and reward-model diagnostics are retained across relocated appendices.

E5.justification: V1's Fleiss-kappa agreement reporting is replaced by raw agreement percentages. V3 additionally reports per-dimension Pearson correlations and Krippendorff alpha for the new quality study, including overall values of 0.41 and 0.73 (Table 5). These revise reliability reporting and are not directly comparable improvements under an unchanged rubric. Neither version reports confidence intervals, significance tests or random seeds.

E6.justification: V3 adds substantial results for new models, quality metrics, snippet budgets and MCP. For example, Gemini's newly reported Distinct3 scores are 1.76 for vanilla and 2.74 for standard Frankentexts; the new 5,000-snippet configuration has 85% coherence and 72% Pangram-human classification (Table 2). MCP configurations report only 43–45% copying (Table 11). The standard Gemini results remain 75% copying, 81% coherence and 59% human classification. V1's 4% pairwise coherence win finding is replaced by quality ratings under a different human-evaluation setting, not a directly comparable performance gain.

T1.justification: Neither version presents formal theorems or proofs. The existing algorithm and trigram-matching/ROUGE-L copy-rate computation are retained. V3's combinatorial-search motivation and descriptions of borrowed evaluation metrics do not add formal complexity results, assumptions or mathematical derivations.

C1.justification: V1 primarily establishes a challenging constrained-generation task, largely coherent outputs and detector vulnerability. V3's abstract, introduction and conclusion promote Frankentexts as an alternative narrative-generation paradigm that surpasses vanilla generation in writing quality, diversity and originality. Its headline Gemini detector-evasion figure changes from 59% to 72% using a new configuration. This substantially strengthens and broadens the claimed contribution.

C2.justification: V3 adds interpretations of snippet-budget gains and their plateau, attributes MCP's reduced copying to increased verbosity, discusses possible judge bias, and qualifies GPT-5's high quality ratings with its low coherence. It also expands the discussion of generation cost, creative recombination and copyright, and adds difficulty measuring diversity as a limitation. Existing explanations of transition problems, grammar errors, nonfiction fabrication and detector weaknesses largely remain.

D1.justification: V3 adds MCP implementation details and its system prompt, the quality-judge and vanilla-generation prompts, GPT-4.1 decoding settings, and expanded cost estimates. Conversely, v1's numerical Binoculars/FastDetectGPT thresholds are no longer documented. V3 removes the repository link and promises code/data release after review, although its conclusion still says they are released. Reproducibility information also contains unresolved inconsistencies: Appendix Q names GPT-4.1 as the alternative judge while Table 12 names GPT-5, and the cost narrative retains a total inconsistent with the revised table.

R1.justification: V3 substantially broadens positioning from controllable generation and mixed-authorship detection toward computational creativity, diversity and copyright. It explicitly contrasts its approach with vanilla autoregressive generation and conventional retrieval-augmented generation, and adds relevant sources including Boden, Buschek, NoveltyBench and copyright scholarship. This exceeds bibliographic formatting changes; much of the earlier collaborative-writing and detection literature remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, evaluation description and results narrative are extensively rewritten around writing quality and originality. Results subsections are reorganized, and human detectability, prompt specificity, limitations and other material move into reorganized appendices. These are substantial narrative and structural revisions beyond the accompanying scientific additions.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column to a single-column layout. Table 2 is substantially redesigned around new quality columns, with detailed detection results separated into Table 8. V3 adds a human-quality ratings chart and agreement, retrieval and judge tables; replaces the pairwise-interface screenshot and several examples; and removes v1's snippet-ablation heatmap. Numerous retained plots are relocated and resized, while the pipeline illustration remains substantially the same.

improvement.justification: V3 provides useful evidence beyond v1's feasibility evaluation through graded human ratings, agreement analysis, diversity measurements and retrieval/scaling tests. However, Section 4.1 claims superiority across all evaluation dimensions despite lower coherence in Table 2, and the new Utility3 evidence relies on WQRM without resolving the retained control where disconnected fragments score 8.494 (Appendix S). Inconsistent judge identification further complicates interpretation. The added evidence and weakened alignment between some central claims and their support leave the net change in overall quality uncertain.
